actions.heading: What to do first, and why
paragraphs: First, expand Kikamba and Luhya training and held-out data, since these have the least headroom over the {F016}% floor. Second, confirm how abstention is scored, then review it for Luhya ({F038}%) and Kiswahili ({F042}%). Changing a threshold before knowing this could move accuracy without improving the model.

Third, commission fresh, independently labelled sealed material before selecting another recipe, because the {F008} held-out units have been inspected. Fourth, change one thing per run. At {F009} GPU-hours a run, this is affordable and lets any change in Kikamba or Luhya be attributed to its cause.

findings_R01_1.heading: Every language clears the floor; two have little headroom
paragraphs: All {F011} of {F012} languages are at or above the {F016}% floor and none falls below the base. The largest gains came where the base was weakest. Kikamba rose from {F021}% to {F019}%, Ekegusii from {F017}% to {F015}%, and Luhya from {F037}% to {F035}%. Gikuyu reached {F023}% from {F025}%, and Kalenjin {F027}% from {F029}%.

Kiswahili is the exception in kind. Its base already scored {F041}%, and the model reaches {F039}%, so the gain there is small. Kikamba and Luhya have the thinnest margins over the floor, and a modest drop on fresh material could take either below it. That is the main reason to prioritise them.

findings_R01_2.heading: Data, compute and abstention behind the result
paragraphs: Training used {F006} units and {F007} tokens of RMS transcripts. Scoring used a sealed held-out set of {F008} units. The record does not split that set by language, so the uncertainty around each per-language figure cannot be stated. This matters most for Kikamba and Luhya, where margins are thin.

The run took {F009} GPU-hours, or {F010} minutes on one GPU. Compute is therefore not the constraint on iteration. Abstention varies from {F026}% for Gikuyu to {F042}% for Kiswahili, with Luhya at {F038}% and Kikamba at {F022}%. The record does not say whether abstentions count as errors in the accuracy figures.

risks.heading: What the record cannot yet establish
paragraphs: Performance outside the measured languages and the sealed set is not established; an independently designed evaluation would close that gap. Independent final acceptance is not possible after further recipe selection on inspected results, and needs fresh, sealed, independently labelled material.

No new production plan is linked to this historical run, so lineage from objective to production is incomplete. Closing it needs an explicitly compiled, evidence-linked objective, never a backdated assumption. Serving is a separate operation: the full adapter is served and the pruned adapter is admitted but not served. The record carries no evidence on privacy handling of the transcripts.

summary: The language identification model was trained for {F004} epochs on {F006} RMS training units ({F007} tokens). It passes all {F011} of {F012} checks: every language is at or above the {F016}% floor, and none has regressed below the base. Macro accuracy rose by {F013} points. The model is recorded as admitted.

The result is strong but uneven in headroom. Kikamba ({F019}%) and Luhya ({F035}%) are closest to the floor, and Luhya abstains on {F038}% of items. The next improvement should therefore be targeted data for those two languages, followed by a review of abstention behaviour.
The held-out results have been inspected, so they cannot count as independent final acceptance for any further recipe choice. This paper covers the retained measurements from this run only.

Second, review abstention for Luhya ({F038}%) and Kiswahili ({F042}%). The record does not show whether abstentions count as errors, so confirm that before changing any threshold.
Third, commission fresh, independently labelled sealed material before choosing another recipe, because the {F008} held-out units have now been inspected.
Fourth, change one thing per run. At {F009} GPU-hours a run, any movement in Kikamba or Luhya can be attributed to a single change.
